title: How an HTTPS (TLS) handshake works
sub: Two strangers agree on a secret key in public, the server proves who it is with a certificate, and then everything is encrypted. Tiny numbers here, same idea as the real thing.
aria: A sequence diagram of a TCP and TLS handshake between a browser and a server with an eavesdropper in the middle
breakLabel: 💥 Break it: skip certificate checks, let an attacker in the middle
breakOff: Normal run: Eve can watch every packet, but only sees public numbers and then ciphertext.
breakOn: Mallory sits on the path and answers with her own key share and a forged certificate. The browser has verification switched off (like curl -k), so it accepts it.
learn: Diffie–Hellman: each side sends g^secret mod p. Both compute the same shared key S, yet a watcher who only sees the public numbers can't easily get it. Here p = 23, g = 5: toy sizes, real ones are enormous.
Change the browser's or server's secret: the public numbers change but both sides still land on the same S.
Slide TLS from 1.2 to 1.3: the handshake drops from two round trips to one, so the first byte arrives a full round trip sooner.
The certificate check is what stops a man-in-the-middle: key exchange alone can't tell you who you agreed a key with.
Break it: the browser and the server end up with different keys, and Mallory holds both, so she reads the password and re-encrypts it for the server.
The cipher drawn here is a toy XOR stream, for illustration only.
